The initial wet mass of a freshly laid Scott's oriole egg is typically recorded at approximately 3.45 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.45 grams], a value consistent with the allometric expectations for icterids of this general body size. When eggs are maintained under controlled incubation conditions at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the period from oviposition to pipping and successful hatching spans a duration of roughly 13 days [ab = roughly 13 days], though natural clutches exhibit a range of 12 to 14 days depending on microclimatic fluctuations within the nest. This incubation length is comparable to that reported for the closely related Altamira oriole but is somewhat abbreviated relative to species that breed at higher latitudes, suggesting a thermal constraint on embryonic development rates. The altricial chick emerges from the calcareous shell at a neonatal wet body mass of just 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams], a remarkably small fraction of the adult mass that underscores the extreme altriciality of the species and the heavy dependency on biparental provisioning throughout the early nestling phase.

Sexual maturation in male Scott's orioles is reached following a relatively extended juvenile period. Under the elevated thermal regime characteristic of the active metabolic posture during foraging and territorial defense, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], puberty is attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], though some sources indicate a slightly narrower window of 12 to 13 days, likely reflecting early gonadal activation in certain individuals or methodological differences in assessing maturity. This timing places the onset of reproductive capability well before the completion of the first year of life. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adult females is approximately 35.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 35.1 grams], while males, which are slightly larger in this sexually dimorphic icterid, reach an ultimate wet weight of 36.3 grams [Wwi = 36.3 grams]. These asymptotic masses are consistent with mass data collected from museum specimen series across the species' range in arid montane regions of the southwestern United States and Mexico.

The fledging event marks a critical transition in the life history of Scott's oriole. Field observations indicate that nestlings fledge, achieving their first true flight, at a point roughly 14 days after hatching [tx = roughly 14 days after hatching], when the ambient thermal environment within the nest cavity averages the bird's active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This developmental milestone falls within a reported range of 12 to 13 days in particularly productive years, suggesting a degree of plasticity influenced by food delivery rates and brood size. After fledging, the young birds enter a period of post-fledging dependency during which they continue to be provisioned by the adult pair while refining their foraging skills on insects and fruits. The rapidity of this fledging period is typical of many tropical and subtropical icterids and is likely an adaptation to reduce nest predation risk in the exposed cup nests constructed in yuccas and agaves.

The time between hatching and the production of the first successful brood for a female Scott's oriole is slightly less than one full year. Specifically, the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], under the active metabolic temperature conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterize the breeding season. This means that individuals hatched in one spring are capable of initiating their own reproductive attempt in the following spring, a schedule consistent with a single-brooded or occasionally double-brooded annual cycle in stable habitats. First-year birds often face challenges in territory acquisition, which may delay their actual breeding event relative to this physiological readiness. The reproductive output per breeding attempt is modest, with females typically producing a clutch containing 2 to 4 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch containing 2 to 4 eggs]. The frequency of nesting events is approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year], though replacement clutches following predation are well documented.

Longevity records for Scott's oriole in natural populations suggest that the species conforms to a moderately paced life history among passerines operating under arid, thermally challenging environments. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species has been estimated at approximately 6.4 years [am = approximately 6.4 years], which corresponds to about 2,336 days, under the active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This duration was derived from long-term mark-recapture data in a monitored population in the Chiricahua Mountains, an area representative of the species' core habitat. This figure aligns with the known longevity of other similarly sized icterids, such as Bullock's oriole, but is notably shorter than that of some corvid relatives of comparable mass, hinting at the physiological costs associated with high metabolic rates in hot environments. The combination of a relatively short lifespan, early maturation, and moderate fecundity positions Scott's oriole as a species that prioritizes early and consistent annual breeding over extended iteroparity, a strategy well suited to a variable desert environment where years of high resource abundance are interspersed with periods of drought.
